Choosing a method

Source: vignettes/articles/choosing-a-method.Rmd
choosing-a-method.Rmd

featR has fourteen selection functions and two dimensionality-reduction functions. Pick one by the question you are asking, then check the reference tables at the end for what it accepts, how it treats missing values, and which optional packages it needs.

Start with the question

Question Function
Which columns are constant, near-constant, or mostly missing? fs_unsupervised()
Which columns duplicate each other? fs_correlation()
Which numeric columns are individually associated with the outcome? fs_supervised()
Which categorical columns are associated with a categorical outcome? fs_chi(), fs_infogain()
How much does each column reduce uncertainty about the outcome, whatever its type? fs_infogain()
Which predictors survive in a sparse linear model? fs_lasso(), fs_elastic()
Which predictors carry any information about the outcome? fs_boruta(); set cutoff_cor = NULL to keep redundant ones too
How does each predictor rank in a random forest, and how good is that forest on held-out rows? fs_randomforest()
Which predictors does a model with automatic non-linearities and interactions use? fs_mars()
What is the smallest subset a particular model needs? fs_recursivefeature(), fs_svm()
Which terms does AIC keep in a linear regression? fs_stepwise()
Which predictor subset has the best out-of-sample predictive fit under a Bayesian model? fs_bayes()
Can I summarize these columns in a few directions? fs_pca(), fs_svd()

The method guides cover each function in depth: Filter methods, Regularization and embedded importance, Wrapper methods, and Dimensionality reduction.

Filters, embedded methods, and wrappers

A filter scores each feature without fitting a predictive model. The filters are fs_unsupervised(), fs_supervised(), fs_chi(), fs_infogain(), and fs_correlation(). They are fast and scale to thousands of columns. The cost is that they look at one feature at a time (or, for fs_correlation(), one pair at a time), so two copies of the same signal both score highly, and a feature that matters only in combination with another scores low. Use filters for a first cut, then refine with something else.

An embedded method fits one model and reads the selection off its structure: non-zero coefficients, importance, or retained terms. The embedded methods are fs_lasso(), fs_elastic(), fs_randomforest(), and fs_mars(). They account for the other predictors, but the answer belongs to that model family. fs_randomforest() ranks rather than selects: unless you pass a selection function in control$feature_select, selected holds every predictor the forest used, in importance order, and the cutoff is yours.

A wrapper refits a model over many candidate subsets. The wrappers are fs_recursivefeature(), fs_svm(), fs_boruta(), fs_stepwise(), and fs_bayes(). They are the most expensive and the most tailored to one model. They are also the most prone to overfitting the selection itself, so validate their output on held-out data.

A sensible default pipeline

For a new tabular problem:

  1. Drop constant or mostly missing numeric columns with fs_unsupervised(). It uses no outcome, so it is safe to run before any split.
  2. Hold out a test set now, before anything looks at the outcome.
  3. Prune near-duplicate numeric columns with fs_correlation() on the training rows.
  4. On the training rows, run the selector that matches your final model: fs_lasso() for a linear model, fs_recursivefeature() (random forests by default) for a forest, fs_svm(feature_select = TRUE) for an SVM. Use fs_boruta(cutoff_cor = NULL) instead when you want every informative feature rather than a compact set.
  5. Evaluate the final model on the test rows.

The validation and leakage article runs this pipeline end to end and lists which numbers each function reports on held-out data.

Reference: what each function accepts

The calling convention is data first, then target as a string for the functions that use an outcome. Four functions break the pattern:

  • fs_svm() requires task = "classification" or "regression" and will not guess it.
  • fs_randomforest() takes task too, defaulting to "classification"; it warns when that default meets a numeric target.
  • fs_bayes() uses only the columns you list in predictors, and fs_svd() takes a numeric matrix x instead of data.

Outcome and predictor types

“Dummy-coded” means factor and character predictors are expanded into one column per level, so selected names those columns (colorred) rather than the original one (color). The fs_result object article lists which functions do this.

Function Outcome (target) task reported Predictor columns
fs_unsupervised() none NA numeric only; any other column is an error
fs_correlation() none NA numeric for "pearson", "spearman", "kendall"; ordered factors for "polychoric"; numeric or two-valued columns for "pointbiserial"
fs_supervised() numeric, factor, character, or logical "regression" for numeric, "classification" for factor, NA for character or logical numeric only; any other column is an error
fs_chi() anything, coerced to a factor (a numeric outcome becomes one class per distinct value) "classification" factor and character only; numeric, logical, and date columns are skipped
fs_infogain() anything; a numeric outcome is binned always "classification" any mix: numeric columns are binned, dates split into year, month, and day
fs_lasso() numeric only "regression" numeric, factor, character, logical; dummy-coded
fs_elastic() numeric, or factor, character, or logical for classification either numeric, factor, character, logical; dummy-coded
fs_randomforest() set by task either numeric, factor, character, logical, Date
fs_mars() numeric, or factor or character for classification; logical is an error either numeric, factor, character, logical; importance is mapped back to the original column
fs_recursivefeature() numeric, or factor, character, or logical for classification either numeric, factor, character, logical; dummy-coded only with handle_categorical = TRUE
fs_svm() set by task; a numeric outcome may be a class label only if it has at most 10 values either numeric, factor, character, logical; dummy-coded
fs_boruta() numeric, or factor for classification; character is an error either numeric, factor, character, logical, Date, POSIXt
fs_stepwise() numeric only "regression" numeric, factor, character, logical; scores are per term, not per dummy
fs_bayes() whatever brm_family accepts (numeric for gaussian(), 0/1 or logical for bernoulli()) "classification" for binary, categorical, and ordinal families, else "regression" the columns named in predictors; date_col adds an iso_week_id predictor
fs_pca() none no fs_result numeric columns; other columns are kept as labels
fs_svd() none no fs_result a numeric matrix, or a data frame whose columns are all numeric

Missing values and optional packages

The packages in the last column are in featR’s Suggests, so they are not installed with featR. Packages listed in parentheses are needed only for the feature named. When a required package is missing, the function stops before doing any work and prints the install.packages() call you need. A few are optional extras with a fallback instead of an error: without bigstatsr, fs_pca() uses prcomp() on large data; without pROC, fs_randomforest() reports no AUC and fs_mars() tunes on accuracy instead of ROC and skips the test ROC AUC; without PRROC, fs_mars() skips the PR AUC; without pbapply, fs_bayes() shows no progress bar. Optional dependencies has one command that installs every suggested package.

Function Missing values Suggests packages
fs_unsupervised() na_rm = TRUE (default) ignores them for "variance", "mad", "iqr", "range"; "missing_prop" and "n_unique" always see them none
fs_correlation() na.rm = FALSE (default) leaves those correlations NA, and an NA pair is never flagged; na.rm = TRUE drops them pairwise. "polychoric" errors unless na.rm = TRUE, then drops incomplete rows polycor ("polychoric"); foreach, doParallel (parallel point-biserial)
fs_supervised() na_rm = TRUE (default) drops incomplete rows separately for each feature none
fs_chi() each feature is tested on its own complete cases furrr, future (parallel = TRUE)
fs_infogain() handled per predictor and outcome pair none
fs_lasso() an error, for the outcome and for predictors; impute = "mean" fills predictors with full-data means and warns that this leaks glmnet; foreach, doParallel (parallel = TRUE)
fs_elastic() rows with any missing value are dropped caret, glmnet, Matrix; e1071 (classification); foreach, doParallel (n_cores > 1)
fs_randomforest() rows with a missing outcome are dropped with a warning; missing predictors are imputed with training-row medians and modes randomForest, caret; pROC (binary AUC); foreach, doParallel (n_cores > 1)
fs_mars() rows with any missing value are dropped caret, earth; e1071 (classification); pROC, PRROC (binary ROC and PR AUC); MLmetrics with pROC (multiclass summary); foreach, doParallel (n_cores > 1)
fs_recursivefeature() an error in the outcome or the training predictors; missing test values are not imputed caret; randomForest (default function set, or model_method = "rf"); e1071 (classification); foreach, doParallel (parallel = TRUE)
fs_svm() an error caret, kernlab; e1071 (classification); randomForest (select_method = "rf_rfe"); foreach, doParallel (n_cores > 1)
fs_boruta() an error Boruta
fs_stepwise() rows with any missing value are dropped, with a warning MASS
fs_bayes() rows missing the outcome, a predictor, or date_col are dropped brms, loo, and a working Stan toolchain; pbapply (progress bar)
fs_pca() rows with a missing numeric value are dropped ggplot2 (plot); bigstatsr (data of 1e7 cells or more, otherwise prcomp() is used)
fs_svd() an error RSpectra (approximate solver only)

seed, parallelism, and which functions use random numbers at all are covered in Reproducibility and parallelism.
